summary:
Space Mission Simulator is a retro pixel-art game that turns the abstract trade-offs of mission design into hands-on decisions. Players plan, build and fly complete missions to the Moon, Mars, the Sun, asteroid Bennu and more.
Each mission starts with an objective and a fixed budget. Players choose the launch vehicle, materials, spacecraft, heat shield, propulsion, power system and payload. Every choice changes mass, cost, delta-v, thrust and power, calculated with real physics such as the rocket equation. A “WHY?” button explains failures without giving the solution away.
Players then pick a safe but costly trajectory or a fast, dangerous one. In flight they manage fuel, food, energy, hull strength and crew health through system failures, real NASA-based solar-flares, repairs, docking and science experiments that balance value against risk. Design Mission mode lets them create their own missions.
The game deliberately mixes realism with fun: alien pirates quizzing players on space facts, a wormhole to a black hole, and arcade mini-games sit alongside real NASA data and mission comparisons. These playful and sci-fi moments draw young people in, and the realistic engineering underneath keeps them learning. Together they spark curiosity and show that space careers are exciting and within reach.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Space Mission Simulator is an interactive game in which players design, manage and fly complete space missions from concept to operation. Each mission takes the player through the full life cycle:

  1. Briefing: real facts about the destination, plus the mission objective, budget and delta-v requirement.
  2. Spacecraft design: choose the launch vehicle size, structural material, spacecraft type, heat shield, launch and spacecraft engines, power system and scientific payload, all within a budget. Every choice changes mass, cost, thrust-to-weight ratio, delta-v, heat resistance, structural strength, power balance and food supply, calculated with real equations such as the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation. A “WHY?” button explains any problem and which parts affect it, without giving away the answer.
  3. Trajectory: choose between a safe but longer and fuel-hungry route and a fast but dangerous direct route.
  4. Launch: a countdown and an ascent through labelled atmospheric layers, with Max-Q, heating, orbit and escape checks.
  5. Operations: a turn-based flight. Players manage fuel, food, energy, hull and crew health while handling system failures, solar flares based on real NASA data, micrometeorites, docking and repairs. Each turn they choose a science experiment, where higher value means a harder challenge.
  6. Arrival: a cargo mini-game (landing, rover driving, orbit insertion and so on), followed by a mission report compared with a real NASA mission.

After a certain point in the game, Design Mission mode unlocks. Players can launch from Earth, the Moon, Mars or Bennu, plan up to five stops with their own budget, and fly them leg by leg using real orbital-transfer maths and gravity assists.

Benefits

  • Turns abstract engineering trade-offs into decisions players can see, test and learn from.
  • Teaches by consequence: poor designs fail in understandable ways, and players iterate.
  • Free and open-source, and runs on any computer with Python.
  • Includes a Fact Book, a sources screen and real-mission comparisons.

Intended impact

To spark interest in space science and engineering among young people, especially students who never get to experience or learn about space missions, and to show that space careers are exciting and achievable. It combines fun gameplay and art style with information and physics to make this learning accessible and engaging.

Tools and technologies

  • Language: Python 3
  • Game library: pygame (pygame-ce)
  • Code hosting: GitHub (public repository)
  • Data: NASA Planetary Fact Sheets, the NASA DONKI space-weather database (solar flares), NASA mission data and the JPL Small-Body Database
  • Art and audio: original pixel art by our design team, designed on Pixilart.com; music and sound effects generated in code
  • SI assistance: Claude: Supported development of code through teaching, converting, debugging and some testing loops; it also created excess designs for time purposes (although as many graphics as possible were designed manually by hand by our graphics team).
  • Hardware: standard laptops (Windows and macOS)

 

Creativity

 

Our Graphics design sub-team created the retro/pixel art style by manually designing, drawing and creating: interfaces, graphics, components, games as well as bringing characters to life through icons, backstory and dialogue.

 

All of the game’s ideas were our own. The core game loop, characters, mini-games and overall concept came from our team’s creative process, which involved many hours of brainstorming, designing and refining.

 

The game mixes realism with fun:

  • alien pirates quiz players on space facts, and a stranded “astronaut” might be an alien impostor;
  • a wormhole leads to a black hole, where players choose to enter it or turn back;
  • arcade mini-games cover docking, wiring repairs and sheltering from radiation.

 

These playful and sci-fi moments sit on top of real physics and NASA data. They draw players in, and the engineering underneath keeps them learning. Simple mini games such as reacting to a solar flare by hiding with food and clothing are realistic reactions and decisions which the player has to make. Aspects like this keep the game engaging and educational.

 

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy vs. simplicity: real physics and data, with clearly labelled game simplifications for budgets and costs.
  • Balance: we tested every possible spacecraft design automatically to make sure each mission is challenging but always possible.
  • Accessibility: retro graphics run on almost any computer, and the tutorial and Mission Control guide new players. While the game does take some time to complete, the effort and thought it takes to design and launch the rocket successfully for each mission pays off. It is unlikely that the player will ever succeed first try, they will spend time designing their rocket to realistic specs, unique to each mission’s requirements.
  • Engagement: short mini-games, varied events and difficulty that increases level by level keep the player engaged through a long process learning different factors of designing and running a space mission
  • Educational value: players are tested only on facts the game has already taught them, so no guessing is needed. Furthermore, the rocket must be designed to match realistic specs, for example while Aluminium may be very light, it could burn up in atmosphere.
